paper_metadata.title: Socioeconomic Differences in Stroke Incidence and Prognosis Under a Universal Healthcare System

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study uses a population-based approach covering all residents of Rome within a specific age range. The use of official municipal and health registries ensures high coverage and minimizes selection bias, as it captures nearly all incident cases in the target population.

items.label: Source of target population
items.prompt: The source population or population of interest is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: all 35- to 84-year-old Rome residents who had a first acute ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke in 2001 to 2004.
items.reasoning: The population is clearly defined by age, geography, and clinical event.

items.label: Method used to identify population
items.prompt: The sampling frame and recruitment are adequately described, including methods to identify the sample sufficient to limit potential bias (number and type used, e.g., referral patterns in health care)
items.evidence_snippet: We collected hospital discharge and mortality data for all... Rome residents... The municipal registry maintains records on all official residents of Rome.
items.reasoning: The study uses a comprehensive administrative registry system which acts as a total population sampling frame.

items.label: Recruitment period
items.prompt: Period of recruitment is adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: occurred from 2001 to 2004
items.reasoning: The four-year window is explicitly stated.

items.label: Place of recruitment
items.prompt: Place of recruitment (setting and geographic location)  are adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: Rome residents... Health Information System of the Lazio region, where Rome is located.
items.reasoning: The geographic setting is clearly defined as the city of Rome, Italy.

items.label: Inclusion and exclusion criteria
items.prompt: Inclusion and exclusion criteria are adequately described (e.g., including explicit diagnostic criteria or “zero time” description).
items.evidence_snippet: ischemic (International Classification of Diseases, 9th Revision 434, 436) or hemorrhagic stroke (International Classification of Diseases, 9th Revision 430, 431)... excluded all hospitalized cases with a secondary diagnosis of late effects... excluded all cases that had heart surgery or a carotid endarterectomy in the previous month
items.reasoning: Detailed ICD-9 codes and specific clinical exclusions are provided to ensure only first-ever incident cases are included.

items.label: Adequate study participation
items.prompt: There is adequate participation in the study by eligible individuals
items.evidence_snippet: The municipal registry maintains records on all official residents of Rome, including mortality information and date and place of death.
items.reasoning: Because this is a registry-based study of all residents, participation is effectively 100% of the eligible population identified through administrative records.

items.label: Baseline characteristics
items.prompt: The baseline study sample (i.e., individuals entering the study) is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Table 1 reports... distribution of total incident cases, out-of-hospital deaths, and hospitalized cases by gender, age, area-based socioeconomic position, and country of birth.
items.reasoning: Key demographic and socioeconomic characteristics are tabulated for the baseline sample.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: Attrition is negligible. Only 11 patients out of over 10,000 were lost to follow-up due to moving out of the region. The use of a mandatory municipal registry for mortality ensures nearly complete follow-up for the primary outcome.

items.label: Proportion of baseline sample available for analysis
items.prompt: Response rate (i.e., proportion of study sample completing the study and providing outcome data) is adequate.
items.evidence_snippet: Nine patients with an ischemic stroke and 2 with a hemorrhagic stroke moved outside of the study area within 1 month after their hospital admission and were lost to follow-up.
items.reasoning: 11/10033 is a loss of approximately 0.1%, which is excellent.

items.label: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out
items.prompt: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out of the study are described.
items.evidence_snippet: The municipal registry maintains records on all official residents of Rome, including mortality information and date and place of death.
items.reasoning: The study design uses continuous registry tracking to minimize dropouts.

items.label: Reasons and potential impact of subjects lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Reasons for loss to follow-up are provided.
items.evidence_snippet: moved outside of the study area
items.reasoning: The specific reason for the very small number of losses is stated.

items.label: Outcome and prognostic factor information on those lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Participants lost to follow-up are adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The characteristics of the 11 lost patients are not described, though the impact is likely zero given the sample size.

items.prompt: There are no important differences between key characteristics (LIST) and outcomes in participants who completed the study and those who did not.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: While not explicitly tested, a 0.1% loss rate is mathematically incapable of introducing significant bias.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Study Attrition Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Loss to follow-up (from baseline sample to study population analyzed) is not associated with key characteristics (i.e., the study data adequately represent the sample) sufficient to limit potential bias to the observed relationship between PF and outcome.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The primary prognostic factor (SEP) is an area-based proxy rather than an individual measure. While validated, the authors acknowledge potential misclassification (ecological fallacy). However, the measurement was applied consistently across the cohort.

items.label: Definition of the PF
items.prompt: A clear definition or description of 'PF' is provided (e.g., including dose, level, duration of exposure, and clear specification of the method of measurement).
items.evidence_snippet: we used a small-area composite index based on 2001 census data (SEP)... education, occupation, home ownership, family composition, and citizenship.
items.reasoning: The SEP index components and construction (factor analysis) are well-defined.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of PF
items.prompt: Method of PF measurement is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: The use of area-based indices as a proxy of individual traits could lead to a misclassification of individual socioeconomic position.
items.reasoning: The index is based on objective census data, but as an area-based proxy, it has inherent validity limitations for individual-level prognosis.

items.prompt: Continuous variables are reported or appropriate cut-points (i.e., not data-dependent) are used.
items.evidence_snippet: distributed in quintiles, ranging from very well off (Level 1) to very underprivileged (Level 5).
items.reasoning: Quintiles are standard, non-data-dependent cut-points.

items.label: Method and Setting of PF Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of measurement of PF is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: We attributed the SEP index to individual cases... through census blocks of residence.
items.reasoning: The same census-based mapping was applied to all participants.

items.label: Proportion of data on PF available for analysis
items.prompt: Adequate proportion of the study sample has complete data for PF variable.
items.evidence_snippet: For each census block with at least 50 inhabitants (4888 census blocks in Rome...)
items.reasoning: The index covered nearly all census blocks; no significant missingness for SEP is reported.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods of imputation are used for missing 'PF' data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The text does not explicitly mention how cases with missing census block information were handled, though it implies high coverage.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: PF Measurement Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: PF is adequately measured in study participants to sufficiently limit potential bias.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: Outcomes (mortality and rehospitalization) are obtained from official administrative registries. These are objective, hard endpoints that are recorded uniformly for all residents, minimizing measurement bias.

items.label: Definition of the Outcome
items.prompt: A clear definition of outcome is provided, including duration of follow-up and level and extent of the outcome construct.
items.evidence_snippet: 30-day mortality, and among 1-month survivors: 1-year mortality, hospital readmissions for a successive stroke, and cardiovascular diseases.
items.reasoning: Outcomes and follow-up durations (30 days, 1 year) are explicitly defined.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Outcome
items.prompt: The method of outcome measurement used is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and confirmation of outcome with valid and reliable test).
items.evidence_snippet: Regional Cause of Death Registry... causes of death coded according to the International Classification of Diseases, 9th Revision
items.reasoning: Registry-based mortality and ICD-coded hospitalizations are standard, reliable methods for outcome ascertainment.

items.label: Method and Setting of Outcome Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of outcome measurement is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: All registries use a personal code that allows a subject to be identified in different registries
items.reasoning: The same regional tracking system was used for the entire cohort.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Outcome Measurement Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Outcome of interest is adequately measured in study participants to sufficiently limit potential bias.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: While the study adjusts for age and identifies several clinical comorbidities, it relies on administrative data for these confounders, which the authors admit may lead to underreporting. Crucially, lifestyle factors (smoking, BMI) were not available for adjustment.

items.label: Important Confounders Measured
items.prompt: All important confounders, including treatments (key variables in conceptual model: LIST), are measured.
items.evidence_snippet: we did not know clinical and lifestyle risk factors, so we could not directly evaluate differences in blood pressure, smoking habits, diet, and physical activity.
items.reasoning: Major lifestyle confounders are missing, though clinical comorbidities were captured via ICD codes.

items.label: Definition of the confounding factor
items.prompt: Clear definitions of the important confounders measured are provided (e.g., including dose, level, and duration of exposures).
items.evidence_snippet: following the definitions of a validated coding algorithm (enhanced Elixhauser AHRQ-Web-ICD-9-CM)
items.reasoning: Clinical confounders are defined using a validated standardized algorithm.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Confounders
items.prompt: Measurement of all important confounders is adequately valid and reliable (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: underreporting of secondary diagnoses and procedures is possible.
items.reasoning: Administrative data is prone to under-coding of comorbidities compared to clinical registries.

items.label: Method and Setting of Confounding Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of confounding measurement are the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: Information on these conditions was found in the clinical records from the index stroke hospitalization and in the records of all hospitalizations that occurred in the 2 years before
items.reasoning: The look-back period and data source were uniform for all cases.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods are used if imputation is used for missing confounder data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The study does not describe handling of missing data for confounders; it likely assumed absence of a code meant absence of the condition.

items.label: Appropriate Accounting for Confounding
items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the study design (e.g., matching for key variables, stratification, or initial assembly of comparable groups).
items.evidence_snippet: stratified by gender... adjusting for age as a continuous variable
items.reasoning: The study uses stratification and multivariable adjustment.

items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the analysis (i.e., appropriate adjustment).
items.evidence_snippet: OR adjusted for age as a continuous variable.
items.reasoning: The primary outcome models (Table 3) are only adjusted for age. While a stratified analysis for clinical risk factors was done, the main results lack multivariable adjustment for comorbidities.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Study Confounding Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Important potential confounders are appropriately accounted for, limiting potential bias with respect to the relationship between PF and outcome.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The statistical methods (Poisson and Logistic regression) are appropriate for the data types. The authors provide sensitivity analyses (Cox models) and account for clustering, which strengthens the validity of the findings.

items.label: Presentation of analytical strategy
items.prompt: There is sufficient presentation of data to assess the adequacy of the analysis.
items.evidence_snippet: We used Poisson models to calculate age-adjusted incidence rates... logistic regression was used to study socioeconomic disparities in short-term and 1-year outcomes
items.reasoning: The analytical plan is clearly laid out for each objective.

items.label: Model development strategy
items.prompt: The strategy for model building (i.e., inclusion of variables in the statistical model) is appropriate and is based on a conceptual framework or model.
items.evidence_snippet: To evaluate whether the effect of SEP on stroke prognosis was possibly mediated by clinical risk factors, we performed a stratified analysis.
items.reasoning: The use of stratification to explore mediation by clinical factors is a sound strategy.

items.prompt: The selected statistical model is adequate for the design of the study.
items.evidence_snippet: Clustering within census blocks was taken into account using robust variance estimation.
items.reasoning: Accounting for the clustered nature of area-based data is a high-quality statistical practice.

items.label: Reporting of results
items.prompt: There is no selective reporting of results.
items.evidence_snippet: Table 3 shows the association... relative frequency of the outcomes (crude risk) and the OR adjusted for age are reported.
items.reasoning: Results for all pre-specified outcomes (mortality and rehospitalization) are reported, including non-significant findings.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Statistical Analysis and Presentation Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: The statistical analysis is appropriate for the design of the study, limiting potential for presentation of invalid or spurious results.
